<reason>Side A (CON) won by maintaining a decisive accessibility argument: prioritizing physical infrastructure inherently excludes commuters, night-shift workers, immunocompromised students, and the severely anxious, while digital expansion reaches excluded students and identifies unmet needs before physical investment. Side B's case that embodied presence is irreplaceable for genuine belonging was strong, but Side A successfully countered that digital platforms can serve as bridges to physical community rather than permanent substitutes, and framed physical-first funding as "selection" rather than "prevention." Side A's sharp pressure questions and direct A1/A2 answers exposed real burdens in Side B's position regarding temporal delays and participation barriers.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Rebuttal 2 answers (A4.1 and A4.6) decisively countered Side B's "bridge requires destination" and "physical spaces notice attendance" arguments by showing that digital platforms can actively route isolated students to named hosts and meetings, while physical spaces only detect absence after repeated attendance that excluded students never achieve.</best_rebuttal>
